questions.question: Find x with x ≡ 2 (mod 3) and x ≡ 3 (mod 5) in the range [0, 14].
options: 2, satisfying only the first congruence in the system
8, since 8 mod 3 = 2 and 8 mod 5 = 3
11, since 11 mod 3 = 2 and 11 mod 5 = 1
13, since 13 mod 3 = 1 and 13 mod 5 = 3

questions.question: What condition must the moduli n₁, n₂, …, nₖ satisfy for CRT to apply?
options: All moduli must be prime numbers strictly greater than two
All moduli must be pairwise coprime (gcd of any pair equals 1)
All moduli must share at least one common prime factor each
All moduli must be powers of the same single prime number p
questions.explanation: CRT requires pairwise coprimality: gcd(nᵢ, nⱼ) = 1 for i ≠ j. Then Z/(n₁·…·nₖ)Z ≅ ⊕ Z/nᵢZ.

questions.question: CRT states that the system of congruences x ≡ aᵢ (mod nᵢ) has what kind of solution?
options: Infinitely many incompatible solutions modulo each individual nᵢ
A unique solution modulo N = n₁·n₂·…·nₖ when nᵢ are pairwise coprime
A unique rational solution that may not be an integer modulo any nᵢ
Exactly k solutions, one for each modulus, that must agree pairwise
questions.explanation: CRT: unique solution in Z/NZ where N = product of nᵢ, given pairwise-coprime moduli.

questions.question: Why does CRT make RSA decryption ~4× faster?
options: It replaces one mod n exponentiation with two half-size mod p, mod q ones
It caches partial products of d mod φ(n) across separate decryptions
It avoids modular exponentiation by precomputing m for every possible c
It runs decryption in parallel by splitting n into k coprime moduli
questions.explanation: Decrypt mod p and mod q separately (each ~|n|/2 bits), then CRT-combine. Each modexp is ~8× cheaper; net ~4× speedup.

questions.question: Garner's algorithm reconstructs x from residues (a₁, …, aₖ) iteratively. Why prefer it over the textbook CRT formula?
options: It avoids computing the full product N = n₁·…·nₖ before reconstruction
It works for non-coprime moduli where the textbook formula fails outright
It uses floating-point arithmetic for speed at the cost of small errors
It returns negative representatives in the symmetric range (−N/2, N/2]
questions.explanation: Garner builds x = a₁ + n₁·(... ) incrementally without computing N explicitly. Better numerical and cache behavior; standard in RSA-CRT implementations.

questions.question: Given x ≡ 1 (mod 5) and x ≡ 2 (mod 7), what is x in [0, 34]?
options: 9, since 9 mod 5 = 4 and 9 mod 7 = 2 only partially
16, since 16 mod 5 = 1 and 16 mod 7 = 2
23, since 23 mod 5 = 3 and 23 mod 7 = 2 fails first congruence
30, since 30 mod 5 = 0 and 30 mod 7 = 2 fails first congruence

questions.question: Why is RSA-CRT signing dangerous without fault protection?
options: A glitch in computing s_p but not s_q lets attacker compute gcd(s^e − m, n) = p
CRT recombination uses Euler's totient which leaks the private exponent d
Garner's algorithm caches m mod p in memory, recoverable via cold-boot
CRT decryption is timing-leaky regardless of constant-time multiplication
questions.explanation: Bellcore attack: if s_p is correct but s_q is faulted, then s^e ≢ m (mod q) but s^e ≡ m (mod p). gcd(s^e − m, n) = p factors n instantly.

questions.question: Hastad's broadcast attack uses CRT against RSA with which weakness?
options: Same plaintext m sent to k recipients with same small e and coprime moduli nᵢ
Same ciphertext c reused across k different keys sharing one prime each
Same private exponent d reused across k separate moduli to save space
Same modulus n shared across k users with different small public exponents e
questions.explanation: If m^e fits in N = n₁·…·nₖ, CRT-combine k ciphertexts to recover m^e over integers, then take the e-th root. Padding (OAEP) defends.
